title: Executive summary
text:
Today, AI assistants connect directly to a user’s private correspondence via a variety of partially and fully supported, secure (and insecure) connectors. Under this status quo, AI providers are empowered to act as fiduciary over this data, to the end of enabling bleeding edge automation and research capabilities to their users. Simply put, users should not need to sign over their data ownership rights in exchange for access to the best AIs. This document proposes a security architecture for a messaging mirror that can be securely, safely and privately operated by the user themselves or by a trusted 3rd party.
The problem. Data ownership is one of the biggest impediments to the proliferation of beneficial AI, especially in security, safety and privacy critical industries. Many individuals and organizations are unwilling to cede their data rights to AI companies. There currently exists no end-to-end security reference architecture to enable individuals or organizations to securely, safely and privately host their own data mirrors in a way that is integrated and compatible with AI assistants. 
The alternative. Without a community effort to develop a security, privacy and safety standard around private data, the most likely outcome is for AIs to continue centralizing power using this strategy. Private 3rd party companies hosting closed source messaging mirrors require the user to trust that bond. The technical requirements of building such data management systems require seasoned, credentialed software engineering veterans. Vibe-coded systems from novices don’t cut it.  
Why this document. I am an engineer with more than 15 years in industry and independent research in machine learning. For the last six months I have worked on delivering AI to businesses safely, securely and privately, and I built a system that does it over a customer’s own messages. Every customer contract turns on the same question: how is their data protected? The industry would benefit from answering that question once, together. This document is my steel-man architecture, the strongest version I can make, for others to attack and improve.
What is asked of you. Attack the design. The threat model (section 4), the search leakage (section 10) and the fourteen open questions (section 16) matter most.

title: 2. Scope
text:
This document covers the server-side copy of each account’s data, which the service calls the mirror, and every credential that can open it.
The system. The client, a desktop app, reads the user’s mail, messages, calendars, contacts and files on the device and uploads a copy to the server: the mirror. AI assistants the user connects, today Claude and ChatGPT, query the mirror over MCP. A web board shows it in a browser. The server also fetches Slack itself, receives inbound email, and runs a Telegram bot.







In scope
What it covers




Content at rest
Messages, chats, contacts, calendar events, attachments, contact photos and uploads, plus records derived from them (triage, matters, people, traces)


Keys and tokens
The account key, its locked copies, every token a holder presents, and the source tokens for Google and Slack


Access paths
The client, AI assistants over MCP and OAuth 2.1, the web board, and company support


Search
Matching and regex search over encrypted content


Backups
Cloud SQL point-in-time recovery and daily backups



Built today versus proposed. Today the mirror’s content is stored in plaintext columns in Cloud SQL (Postgres 15) and objects in Cloud Storage, under Google’s default encryption at rest. All traffic uses TLS. Tokens are stored as SHA-256 hashes. Google grants are encrypted with one server-wide key. Today, the service’s administrators can read or change any account’s mirror through the service’s own routes, and the service keeps no audit record of which administrator did so. Everything in sections 6 to 10 is proposed and not built.
Phasing. Accounts that use only the client switch first. The server does no background AI work for them (triage, filing, briefs), so it reads their content only while answering a request or taking an upload. Accounts that use the web board’s background features follow once section 16’s questions on them are settled.
Out of scope: the security of the user’s device beyond the client’s use of the OS keystore; what AI providers do with answers they receive; the original sources (Gmail, Microsoft 365, iMessage, WhatsApp, Slack, Telegram); transport security beyond requiring TLS; and availability.

title: 3. System overview
text:
The server holds K only inside a request that presents a holder’s token and secret. Storage, backups and logs hold ciphertext, keyed tags and token hashes.

Trust assumptions

The device is not compromised when the client first runs, and the OS keystore protects the key at rest.
The Cloud KMS HSM never releases the support key’s private half.
Google Cloud’s infrastructure does not attack the running server. Level 3 removes this assumption for the server.
AES-256-GCM, HKDF-SHA256, HMAC-SHA256, X25519 and RSA-OAEP are secure at the parameters in section 6.
Every connection uses TLS 1.2 or later.
The account holder, signed in, is the person who approves a new AI on the consent page.

title: 5. Security goals and non-goals
text:
This is server-side encryption under keys the user’s holders control. It is not end-to-end encryption: the server decrypts, in memory, for each authorized request.
Goals








#
Goal
Where it is met




G1
Without a holder’s token, stored content, contacts and calendars are ciphertext to everyone, operator staff and anyone with the database, backups or storage included.
Sections 6, 7, 10


G2
Each holder has its own locked copy. Revoking a holder deletes one row and ends its access at once.
Sections 7, 8


G3
Support can read an account only after the user turns on Debug access. It is time-limited, revocable, logged by a party other than the operator, and every use is shown to the user.
Section 9.6


G4
The operator cannot re-read the user’s original sources: the Google and Slack tokens are locked under the account key.
Section 8


G5
Deleting the account deletes every live copy of the key, and the Vault deletes K from the Keychain. Backups keep locked copies until they expire, within 30 days.
Section 9.8


G6
One account’s ciphertext and tags cannot be read or matched with another account’s keys.
Sections 6, 10


G7
An authorized AI’s answer costs about what it costs today.
Section 11


G8
People outside the company can check the code, the build and, at level 3, the running server.
Section 14



Non-goals








#
Not promised
Why




N1
Protecting plaintext in server memory during an authorized request from a compromised server
Needs attestation, level 3


N2
Controlling what an AI provider does with an answer
Outside the operator’s control


N3
Hiding metadata: timestamps, sizes, counts, access times, and which rows share a keyed fragment
Needed for search and ordering (section 10)


N4
Protecting backups taken before cutover
They expire within 30 days


N5
Defending against malware on the user’s device
The device holds the key


N6
Keeping the mirror readable if every holder is lost
No recovery key exists. The mirror refills from the original sources.

One account key, K, encrypts everything, and each holder reaches it only through a copy wrapped under its own secret.

title: 9. Protocol flows
text:
9.1 Enrollment: the client’s first run
The eight flows below are the whole proposal: in each, K is unwrapped only inside a request that presents a holder’s secret. Notation is from section 6. Steps marked “built” run that way today.
The first three messages run today; everything below the line is proposed. K is created on the device, and only locked copies cross to the server.

title: 9. Protocol flows
text:
Client → Server: sign in with Google or an emailed code. Built.
Server → client: device token Tₘ. The server stores SHA-256(Tₘ). Built.
Client: generates K, an X25519 keypair (pk, sk), and the device’s unlock secret sₘ.
Client: stores K, Tₘ and sₘ in the OS keystore.
Client → Server: Cₘ = Wrap(HKDF(sₘ), K), pk, and sk encrypted under K.
Server: stores them. K, sk and sₘ never leave the device in the clear.




enrollment sequence · 4 parties, built vs proposed

title: 9. Protocol flows
text:
9.2 Opening the web board

Client → Server: request a connect code, presenting Tₘ and sₘ. Built, without sₘ.
Server → client: a 60-second, single-use connect code. Built.
Client: opens the browser with the code in the URL fragment. Built.
Browser → Server: redeem the code, from a trusted Origin. Built.
Server: makes the session’s secret sₑ and its copy Cₑ.
Server → Browser: an HttpOnly session cookie carrying Tₑ and sₑ.

Whether Cₑ is made at step 2 or step 5 is open (question 6). Made at step 5, a code that expires unused leaves no copy behind, but the code must then carry a secret that opens K.



opening the board · 3 parties, 6 steps


The device vouches for the browser with a one-use code; the browser then holds its own secret in an HttpOnly cookie.

title: 9. Protocol flows
text:
9.3 Connecting an AI assistant (OAuth 2.1)

AI → Server: dynamic client registration, then a redirect to /authorize with a PKCE S256 challenge. Built.
User, signed in on the board, approves on the consent page. Built.
Server: unwraps K through the session’s copy, makes sₐ for the AI, stores Cₐ.
Server → AI: an authorization code, 300 seconds, single use. Built.
AI → Server: /token with the code and the PKCE verifier. Built.
Server → AI: an access token and a refresh token, each carrying sₐ.
On renewal, AI → Server: /token with the refresh token, which carries sₐ, so Cₐ stays openable (question 7).

Today the redirect allowlist admits Claude, ChatGPT and loopback clients only.



connecting an AI · 4 parties, OAuth 2.1 with PKCE


The copy is made inside the user’s signed-in session, so approving the AI is the only step the user takes.

title: 9. Protocol flows
text:
9.4 An AI asks a question

AI → Server: an MCP call, Authorization: Bearer carrying Tₐ and sₐ. Built, without sₐ.
Server: finds the holder by SHA-256(Tₐ), and its copy Cₐ. Built, without Cₐ.
Server: K = Unwrap(HKDF(sₐ), Cₐ), held in a request-scoped context. A route that needs K and lacks it fails; it never falls back to plaintext.
Server → Postgres: look up the query’s keyed tags in the GIN index (section 10).
Postgres → Server: candidate rows, still ciphertext.
Server: decrypts only the candidates, runs the real regex, and returns the answer.
The request ends. K and the plaintext are dropped; nothing is written or logged in the clear.




an AI asks · 3 parties, one request


Only the candidate rows are decrypted, and K is dropped when the request ends.

title: 9. Protocol flows
text:
9.5 Arrivals while nobody is calling

Slack sync, the inbound email webhook or the Telegram bot → Server: a new message. Built.
Server: seals it to pk with HPKE and stores the sealed record. The plaintext exists in memory only while it is sealed.
On the next holder’s call, the server unwraps K, decrypts sk, opens the sealed records, tags them and re-encrypts them under K.

The arrivals queue, which runs on Google Pub/Sub in development, carries message ids only, never content.



arrivals · 4 parties, seal now, open later


New mail keeps arriving without the server ever holding K; it waits sealed until a holder calls.

title: 9. Protocol flows
text:
9.6 Debug access

User, signed in (the session holds K) → Server: turn on Debug access, with an end time and an optional reason.
Server: Cₛ = RSA-OAEP(support public key, K), stored with its expiry.
Support staff, with the IAM role and two-step sign-in → Server: a support request.
Server → Cloud KMS: decrypt Cₛ. KMS → Server: K, for that request. Cloud Audit Logs records the call.
Server → User: the use appears in the user’s list, read from the audit log.
At the end time, or when the user turns it off, the server deletes Cₛ.

Cloud KMS does not know the end time; the server enforces it by deleting the copy (question 8).



Debug access · 4 parties, user-granted and logged


Support has no copy until the user turns access on, and the KMS audit log records each use.

title: 9. Protocol flows
section: 9.7 A lost device, and a new one
text:
9.7 A lost device, and a new one

User, on the board → Server: remove the lost device. The server deletes Cₘ and revokes Tₘ.
New device → Server: sign in and ask to join. The new device shows a short code.
User, on an existing holder: compares the code and approves.
Server: makes a copy for the new device under its own new secret.
If no holder is left, the mirror cannot be read. The new device makes a new K and refills the mirror from the original sources.

How a second device joins, and whether it also keeps K locally, is not specified yet (question 4).



a lost device, and a new one · 3 parties


Revoking a device is deleting one copy; a new device needs approval from a holder the user still has.

title: 9. Protocol flows
text:
9.8 Disconnect, sign out, delete

Disconnect an AI: delete Cₐ, and revoke its access and refresh tokens.
Sign out on the device: revoke Tₘ and the board sessions it opened, and delete their copies.
Delete the account: delete every copy and every row. The Vault deletes K from the Keychain. Backups still hold locked copies until they expire, within 30 days, so a holder secret that survives the deletion could open them until then.




disconnect, sign out, delete · 3 parties


Every exit works by deleting the live copies of K. Backups keep older copies until they expire, within 30 days.

title: 10. Searching encrypted data
text:
Search runs over keyed 64-bit trigram tags, so the database index never holds plaintext. The price is a leakage profile, listed below, and it is the design’s main weakness against a storage thief (A1).
Construction

kₛ = HKDF-SHA256(K, info = “search”, version). A separate key, kᵢ, is derived the same way for identity tags.
For each indexed field (message text, sender, sender name, chat name, participants, alias names), every distinct three-character fragment t gives the tag trunc₆₄(HMAC-SHA256(kₛ, field ‖ t)).
A row’s tags are stored as a bigint[] column with a GIN index. They replace today’s pg_trgm indexes.
A query’s regex is reduced to the fragments any match must contain, the approach of Russ Cox’s trigram index. Those fragments become tags, and the GIN index returns candidate rows.
The server decrypts the candidates and runs the real regex. A truncation collision only adds a false candidate, which this check removes.
A pattern with no required fragment, such as .*, falls back to a bounded scan of the most recent rows.
Handles, addresses and names are normalized and tagged under kᵢ, so conversations and the people graph can be grouped without plaintext.

What an adversary with the database learns








Leak
Who sees it
Severity




Each row’s number of distinct fragments, roughly its length
A1, A2
Low

A1, A2
Medium. Frequency analysis and known plaintext can recover common fragments: see the leakage-abuse and inference attacks in section 18.


Which tags a live query touched (the access pattern)
Anyone watching the database while queries run

A1, A2
Low to medium

Nobody
None: the tag keys differ per account



A concrete case: a thief who also knows a newsletter that an account received can mark that newsletter’s tags and look for them in the account’s other rows. Section 16, question 5, asks whether padding or bucketing the tag sets is worth its cost.

title: 11. Performance
text:
The design adds an estimated few milliseconds to each authorized request, mostly the regex recheck. K is opened in memory once per request with no network call, and only the rows in the answer are decrypted.

These are estimates, not measurements. Before anything switches over, the search work will measure them on a synthetic account the size of the largest real one, about 1.6 million messages, and publish the results here.

Until level 3, that build sees plaintext during requests


R1
Repudiation
TB6
Support denies having read an account
Every KMS decrypt is in Cloud Audit Logs and shown to the user
Expiry is enforced by the server, not KMS


I1
Information disclosure
TB4
Database, backup or bucket theft
Content encrypted; tags keyed per account; tokens stored as hashes
Metadata and tag overlap (section 10); backups taken before cutover


I2
Information disclosure
TB4
Content written to logs
A key context that never logs; a test that scans the server’s log calls for content
A logging change that the test misses


I3
Information disclosure
In process
Memory read on a compromised server
K lives for one request
Not defended until level 3


I4
Information disclosure
TB7
Source tokens used to re-read the originals
Google and Slack tokens wrapped under K
None, once built


D1
Denial of service
All
Every holder is lost
The mirror refills from the original sources
Data that exists only on the server, if stored under K


D2
Denial of service
TB5
Cloud KMS is unavailable
KMS is used only for Debug access
Support is delayed

Elevation of privilege
TB2, TB3
A bug serves another account’s rows
Per-account keys: the rows do not decrypt under the caller’s K
A bug in the key context itself


E2

title: 13. Residual risks and known limitations
text:
The design leaves fourteen known weaknesses, listed here so no reader has to discover them. The first three matter most.









#
Limitation
Consequence
What would close it




L1
The server holds K and plaintext in memory during each authorized request
A compromised server or a malicious build can copy them (T3, I3)
Attestation, level 3


L2
Search tags leak which rows of an account share a fragment
A storage thief with some known plaintext can infer more (section 10)
Padding or bucketing tag sets (question 5)


L3
Backups taken before cutover hold plaintext
Readable by a backup thief until they expire, within 30 days
Time


L4
AI providers see what they ask for
Their handling is outside this design
None here


L5
Metadata stays visible: timestamps, sizes, counts, access times
Traffic analysis of one account
Not planned


L6
The promise depends on locking the source tokens
Without it, the operator could re-read Gmail, Drive, Calendar and Slack directly
Locking Google and Slack tokens under K, before launch


L7
Whoever controls the device at first run controls K
Malware at enrollment owns the key
A hardware-backed or user-presence gate on the OS keystore item (planned, not designed here)


L8
A board session opened from an unlocked device has full device rights
Someone at the device can open the mirror
Narrower session scopes


L9
A hijacked browser session can approve a new AI
The attacker becomes a key holder
An email to the user on every new connection (planned)


L10
Refresh tokens carry the AI’s secret
A leaked refresh token is a long-lived key
Refresh-token expiry and binding (questions 7 and 13)


L11
Debug access expiry is enforced by the server, not by Cloud KMS
A server bug could extend support access
KMS-side conditions (question 8)


L12
Arrivals are in server memory, in the clear, before sealing
A compromised server sees new mail as it arrives
Attestation, level 3


L13
Background features that need content (triage, filing, briefs) cannot run without a caller
Board accounts are not covered by the first phase
Question 12


L14
No recovery key exists
Losing every holder loses data that exists only on the server
A user-held recovery key, if wanted


L15
Revocation and account deletion are enforced by the server, not by cryptography
A backup taken earlier still holds the locked copies, so a holder secret that survives can open it until the backup expires, within 30 days
Rotating K on revocation (question 3), or shorter backup retention



This is server-side encryption, not end-to-end encryption. Readers who need the server never to see plaintext should treat L1 as decisive until level 3 ships.

title: 14. Verification and transparency
text:
Encryption alone still asks users to trust the operator. Three levels make the claims checkable from outside; levels 1 and 2 are proposed for the first release, and level 3 as its own project.









Level
The operator does
Outsiders can check
Does not prove




1. Review
Publishes the key-handling code and this design. Commissions an independent cryptography review and publishes the report.
That the design and the code are sound
That the server runs that code


2. Transparency
Builds each release reproducibly (SLSA), signs it with Sigstore cosign, records it in the Rekor public log, and reports the running image digest on /health. A Verify page in the client lists every key holder and every support use, from the KMS audit log.
That each release is a logged build, and who can open their key
That the running process is that build


3. Attestation
Runs the server in Google Confidential Space on AMD SEV-SNP. Each locked copy is wrapped a second time under a server key that Cloud KMS releases only to the attested image digest. The client checks the attestation before it issues a token.
That the server runs that build and cannot be logged into, by the operator included. A stolen token is useless on any other build.
Moving the server from an SSH-managed VM to a sealed container is a project of its own



The chain from source to running server

Public source: the key-handling code, the token handling, the encrypted column type and the search tags.
A reproducible build: the same source always yields the same image digest.
Signed and logged: each release digest is signed and entered in a public transparency log.
An attested server: a confidential VM proves its digest, and keys are released only to it.

At each link, someone outside can check without trusting the operator. A reviewer reads the source. Anyone rebuilds it and compares the digest with the public log and with /health. The user’s client verifies the attestation.

title: 15. Implementation status and roadmap
text:
None of the twenty pieces below is built. They group into roughly ten pull requests, and client-only accounts switch first.










#
Group
Piece
What it does
Technology




1
Keys and tokens
Account key
Made by the client on first run and kept in the OS keystore; one per account
Native client code, platform cryptography library, OS keystore


2
Keys and tokens
Locked copies
One copy per holder, in a table listing its holder, creation time and expiry
HKDF-SHA256, AES key wrap (RFC 5649)


3
Keys and tokens
Tokens that carry the secret
Device tokens, OAuth tokens and the board’s session cookie each carry their holder’s secret; the server keeps only a hash
OAuth 2.1, SHA-256


4
Keys and tokens
Request key context
Opens K once per request and holds it only for that request; a route that needs K and lacks it fails, never falling back to plaintext
FastAPI dependency, contextvars


5
Storage
Encrypted column type
One column type for text and JSON, on every content column, bound to account, table, column and row
SQLAlchemy TypeDecorator, AES-256-GCM


6
Storage
Content coverage test
Reads the models and fails if any content column is stored in the clear, so a column added later cannot slip through
Static (AST) test


7
Storage
Encrypted files
Attachments, contact photos and uploads encrypted before upload, in chunks for large files
Cloud Storage, streaming AES-256-GCM


8
Search
Keyed search tags
Replace today’s trigram indexes (section 10)
HMAC-SHA256, Postgres GIN


9
Search
Query planner
Regex to required fragments, candidate lookup, decrypt and recheck, bounded fallback scan
Python regex parser


10
Search
Keyed identity tags
Handles, addresses and names matched by keyed tag, so grouping and the people graph keep working
HMAC-SHA256


11
No request open
Sealed arrivals
Slack sync, inbound email and the Telegram bot seal each arrival to the account’s public key
HPKE (RFC 9180), X25519


12
No request open
Key-gated jobs
Work that needs content runs only inside a request that holds K
The existing job runner


13
No request open
Locked source tokens
Google and Slack tokens wrapped under K
AES key wrap


14
Access and cutover
Debug access
The Settings control, the support key, an expiry, revocation, and a list of every use shown to the user
Cloud KMS HSM, RSA-OAEP, Cloud Audit Logs


15
Access and cutover
Operator routes
Admin export and raw SQL routes need a key like everything else, and return ciphertext without one
Existing routes


16
Access and cutover
Backfill and cutover
At each device’s next check-in: encrypt existing rows, build tags, then drop the plaintext columns and old indexes
Alembic, a batch job


17
Access and cutover
Public documents
The privacy policy, terms, and the key-custody statements
Documents


18
Portability
Written wire format
Versioned envelopes for locked copies, content, sealed arrivals and tag derivation, with test vectors every client must pass
A specification


19
Portability
One shared core library
The cryptography written once, so a client on another platform writes only its key storage
Rust, with Swift, C# and Linux bindings


20
Portability
Device enrollment
A second device, on any platform, joins through an existing holder (question 4)
—



Why client-only accounts go first. The server already does no background AI work for them, so it reads their content only inside a request or an upload. Accounts that use the board’s background features follow once question 12 is settled.
Other platforms. The server never knows what kind of device a holder is, so a client on another platform producing the same bytes is one more holder. Only key storage differs: Credential Manager or DPAPI with a TPM on Windows, and the Secret Service with TPM2 sealing on Linux. Linux desktop keyrings are often readable by any process in the session, so a Linux client needs TPM sealing or a passphrase to match the guarantee of the other platforms.
Fixes to today’s code. Writing this document surfaced weaknesses in today’s token handling that would undercut the design. They are being fixed before any piece above is built. Under coordinated disclosure, each is listed in the revision history once its fix ships.

title: 16. Questions for reviewers
text:
These fourteen points are where review is wanted most. Comment on a question directly, or anywhere else in the document.

Token format. A holder presents Tₕ and sₕ together in one bearer value. Is that sound, or should sₕ travel separately so that a leaked lookup token alone is useless?
Nonce budget. K encrypts every content value for the life of the account, with random 96-bit GCM nonces. NIST SP 800-38D limits random nonces to 2³² uses per key, and the largest account holds about 1.6 million messages across several columns. Per-table keys derived by HKDF, AES-GCM-SIV, or XAES-256-GCM?
Rotating K. Re-encrypt the mirror, or keep content under data keys wrapped by K, so that rotation re-wraps only keys?
A second device. Is comparing a short code on an existing holder enough to admit a new device? Should the new device receive K itself, and over what channel?
Search leakage. Is a keyed 64-bit trigram index acceptable for this threat model? Are padded tag sets or bucketed fragments worth their cost in index size and false candidates?
The board session’s copy. Make it when the connect code is minted, deleting it if unredeemed, or when the code is redeemed, which needs the code to carry a secret?
Refresh. Carry sₐ inside the refresh token, or re-wrap Cₐ under a fresh secret at each refresh?
Debug access expiry. Is deletion by the server enough, or should the KMS decrypt permission carry an IAM condition that ends at the same time?
HPKE on the server. Which maintained HPKE implementation should a Python 3.11 server use?
Verification for the first release. Are levels 1 and 2 enough to ship, with level 3 to follow?
Wire format. Beyond versioned envelopes and test vectors, what must the specification fix so that independent clients interoperate safely?
Background features. Triage, filing and briefs need content when no holder is calling. Run them only on a holder’s call, on the user’s device, or not at all for encrypted accounts?
Token lifetimes. Now that every token carries a key, what expiry and renewal should device, access, refresh and session tokens have?
Recovery. Should users be offered a recovery key they hold themselves, accepting that it can be lost or stolen?

title: 17. Vulnerability disclosure
text:
Report a security problem in the running service privately, never in a comment here. Comments on this document are for the design.

Where to report: open question; a reporting address is still to be named.
What the operator’s security policy commits to: an acknowledgement within 2 business days, an assessment within 5, and a fix for a critical or high-severity issue within 7 days of confirming it, or a stated reason and date.
Safe harbour: good-faith research that follows the policy is treated as authorized, with no legal action.
Please include: what the issue is and what an attacker gains, exact steps to reproduce, the host you tested, and anything you reached that was not yours.
Out of scope: denial-of-service and high-rate automated scanning, social engineering, physical attacks, and third-party services the operator does not run.
Payment and credit: there is no bug bounty. You are credited by name in the fix if you want to be.

Open question: a security.txt (RFC 9116) on the service’s domain, so researchers find this contact without the document.

Glossary







Term
Meaning




Mirror
The server-side copy of an account’s mail, messages, calendars, contacts and files


Client
The desktop app that reads the user’s sources on the device and uploads the mirror


Board
The web interface that shows the mirror in a browser


Holder
Anything that can open K: the device, a connected AI, a board session, a personal access token, or support during Debug access


K, account key
The 256-bit key that encrypts one account’s mirror


Locked copy, Cₕ
K wrapped under a key derived from one holder’s unlock secret


Unlock secret, sₕ
A 256-bit random secret carried only inside a holder’s token


Keyed tag
A truncated HMAC of a text fragment or an identity, under a key derived from K


Sealed arrival
A message encrypted to the account’s public key while no holder is calling


Debug access
A user-controlled, time-limited grant that lets support open the account through Cloud KMS


MCP
Model Context Protocol, the interface AI assistants use to query the mirror

title: Appendix A — Appendix A. Submission process
text:
A change counts as submitted, and is credited, only when it arrives signed by its author through one of the channels below. A name typed into a commit, an email or a comment is never evidence of who wrote it.
The rule. Attribution comes from a cryptographic signature, or from an account the platform has authenticated, never from text. Git author names, Co-authored-by lines, email From headers and names in a document can all be typed by anyone.
Channels









Channel
Counts as
Attributed to
Verified by




GitHub pull request, every commit signed
An official text change
The GitHub account whose registered GPG or SSH key signed each commit
GitHub’s Verified mark, plus a required check that fails on any commit without a verified signature


GitHub issue, from the submission template
An official comment or objection
The GitHub account that opened it
GitHub’s sign-in. At intake the issue’s text is hashed into the submission log, so a later edit shows.


Signed email to the submissions address
An official submission, for people without GitHub
The holder of the signing key or identity
An S/MIME or OpenPGP signature, or a Sigstore signature bound to a verified email. The editor files it as an issue with the signature attached, so anyone can check it.


Google Doc or Claude Doc comment, unsigned email, DOCX
Discussion only
Not attributed
It becomes a submission when its author files it through a channel above



Steps

Discuss anywhere. Discussion is welcome, but it is not a submission.
Submit through a signed channel. A pull request carries a Signed-off-by line under the Developer Certificate of Origin, which licenses the change under CC BY 4.0. That line is a licence, not proof of identity.
Intake. Each submission gets a number, from S-0001, in SUBMISSIONS.md: its channel, its account or key fingerprint, its time, and the SHA-256 of its content.
Disposition. The editor records accepted, declined with a reason, or deferred, as a signed commit naming the submission number.
Merge. Pull requests merge with a merge commit only. Squash and rebase merges rewrite the submitter’s commits, so their signatures would no longer cover what lands. The editor’s own changes are separate signed commits, so readers can always tell the submitter’s words from the editor’s.
Release. Each version is a signed Git tag. Its commit hash is recorded in Sigstore’s public Rekor log and the tagged tree is saved to Software Heritage, so history cannot be quietly rewritten later, by the editor or by GitHub.
Credit. The contributor list is generated from the verified signatures in the history, never typed by hand.

Attacks on attribution, and what stops them







Attack
Control




Committing under someone else’s name or email
Unsigned commits are refused. Submitters should turn on GitHub’s vigilant mode, so anything unsigned under their email shows as Unverified.


Claiming in a description to be someone else
Attribution comes from the signing account, never from text


The editor changing a submitter’s text before merging
Submitter commits merge unchanged; the editor’s edits are separate signed commits, visible in the diff


Forged Co-authored-by or Signed-off-by lines
Never used for attribution


Spoofed email
Only signed email counts


Rewriting history
A protected main branch: signed commits required, no force-push, no deletion. Tag hashes in Rekor. Copies in Software Heritage.


Deleting or editing a comment in a shared document
Those comments are discussion, not submissions


Many accounts posing as broad support
Submissions are weighed on their merit, never counted as votes



What it cannot stop. If a submitter’s own account or signing key is stolen, the thief can submit as them. Use two-factor authentication and, ideally, a hardware security key. A submitter who finds a submission they did not make can disown it with a signed statement, and it is marked disputed.
Open question: the public repository, its branch protection, the signature check, the issue template and the submissions address must exist before the comment period opens.
